summary: Principal Enterprise AI Architect who identified Fishbowl's need for an internal AI platform, made the build-versus-buy case to leadership, and built Atlas from the ground up. Its foundation is a governed MCP gateway of 177 tools across 25 provider modules that carries each employee's own identity and permissions into Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, and other clients. On top of it, Atlas Studio gives non-technical employees desktop and browser chat, reusable skills, scheduled agents, and hosted employee-built apps on one runtime, one identity, and one approval model, with provider-agnostic model routing underneath. Engineering also gets a sandboxed agentic coding pipeline. Applied AI Hackathon winner with deep frontend roots, including MicroFrontend solutions that unify disparate technology stacks.

roles.title: Principal Enterprise AI Architect
responsibilities: Identified the need for an internal agent harness, made the build case to Fishbowl leadership, and secured approval to build rather than buy. Ran a structured build, buy, and hybrid evaluation that included Glean and RunLayer and scored each layer by swap cost, not feature count, then built Atlas around five replaceable seams: model, tools, surface, execution, and memory.

Built the Atlas Gateway, the foundation of every Atlas surface: 177 tools across 25 provider modules, including 57 Fishbowl inventory and manufacturing tools no vendor sells, such as bills of material and landed cost. It speaks plain MCP, so the same governed tools are live in Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity, and Pi, and a new client is a connector entry, not a migration.

Made the gateway act as the employee, never a service account: a per-turn token carries each person's identity so Jira and audit logs see a person, tool lists come from directory groups, and each tool declares read or write to set its approval tier. A declarative connector framework cut the Salesforce connector 87% to about 1KB, with 280+ tests.

Built Atlas Studio so non-technical employees reach those tools through six surfaces on one runtime, identity, and approval model. Chat runs in the browser and a Rust-based Tauri desktop shell with a signed auto-updater, on a Vercel AI SDK tool loop where reads flow freely and writes pause for approval. Every model call is a named LiteLLM route, so a model change is one config line.

Built Skills, versioned instructions employees write and attach to chat, and Agents, automations that run on a schedule. Treated unattended execution as its own security domain: an empty tool allowlist is merely permissive with a person present but dangerous unattended, so the database schema requires every scheduled agent to name its tools and makes skipping approval unreachable.

Built Apps: an employee builds a web app, Atlas hosts it as a single-spa micro-frontend, and a bridge injected at runtime lets it call the same federated tools as the person using it, with a consent step and the same permissions and audit trail. The employee needs no API keys, service account, backend, or deployment. An Admin surface tracks adoption, spend, and outcomes.

In its first eleven days in production (mid August 2026), 65 of Fishbowl's 222 employees used Atlas chat, 85% returned on a different day, 41 were active on three or more days, and at least 25 worked outside engineering. Built in four months: 1,854 commits across four core repositories, about 150K lines of TypeScript and Python, and 506 test files.

Built Atlas Builder for the engineering org, which takes a ticket through a sandboxed, test-driven run to a draft merge request. A harness-neutral supervisor hands each phase to a pluggable coding harness behind a schema-validated contract that rejects malformed output, and checkpoints so runs survive pod loss. Each run gets a per-session Kubernetes sandbox with brokered short-lived credentials.
